original_question: In higher dimensions, does there exist a counterexample to the Ball-Evans approximation problem at some exponent p >= floor(n/2)? Equivalently, can one construct a Sobolev homeomorphism in such a regime that cannot be approximated by diffeomorphisms or piecewise affine homeomorphisms in the relevant Sobolev norm?
target_in_paper: Section 2, Open problem 3 (“Possible counterexample for p ≥ [n/2]”), read together with the definition of the Ball-Evans approximation problem in Section 1, the higher-dimensional formulation in Open problem 1, the non-equivalence issue raised in Open problem 2, and the known counterexamples in Theorem 2.2.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the paper’s target as the open question of whether the known higher-dimensional counterexample range can be extended up to or beyond the threshold p ≥ ⌊n/2⌋. It also correctly interprets a “counterexample to the Ball-Evans approximation problem” as the existence of a Sobolev homeomorphism that cannot be approximated in the Sobolev topology by the admissible regular homeomorphisms.
missing_details: The paper’s setting should be stated explicitly: an open set Ω ⊂ R^n, a homeomorphism f: Ω → f(Ω) ⊂ R^n, and f ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω, R^n).
“Higher dimensions” should be made explicit as the higher-dimensional Ball-Evans problem discussed in the paper, namely n ≥ 3.
The quantifier is existential: one asks whether there exist some dimension n, some exponent p ≥ ⌊n/2⌋, some open set Ω, and some Sobolev homeomorphism f giving a counterexample.
The approximation topology should be named explicitly as strong approximation in the W^{1,p} norm; “the relevant Sobolev norm” is too vague.

The paper treats approximation by diffeomorphisms and approximation by piecewise affine homeomorphisms as two related versions of the problem; for n ≥ 3 their equivalence is not proved and is itself separated out as Open problem 2.

The nearby context matters: Theorem 2.2 gives counterexamples only for n ≥ 4 and 1 ≤ p < ⌊n/2⌋, via sign-changing Jacobian; Open problem 3 asks whether any counterexample exists at or above the threshold, possibly by a different mechanism.

At the borderline p = ⌊n/2⌋ the paper separately asks whether the Jacobian can change sign (Open problem 9), so the refined question should remain about failure of approximation, not collapse into the narrower Jacobian-sign problem.
refined_question: Does there exist a higher-dimensional counterexample to the Ball-Evans approximation problem at or above the threshold p = ⌊n/2⌋? More precisely, do there exist n ≥ 3, an open set Ω ⊂ R^n, an exponent p ≥ ⌊n/2⌋, and a homeomorphism f: Ω → f(Ω) ⊂ R^n with f ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω, R^n) such that f is not the strong W^{1,p}-limit of a sequence of diffeomorphisms, or alternatively of a sequence of piecewise affine homeomorphisms?
justification: The nearest official formulation is Open problem 3 in Section 2, whose wording is essentially: is it possible to construct a counterexample to the Ball-Evans approximation problem for some p ≥ [n/2] in higher dimensions? This is exactly the issue your draft is aiming at. To make it stand-alone and paper-faithful, one has to restore the ambient Sobolev setting f ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω, R^n), the existential quantifiers over n, p, Ω, and f, and the fact that the approximation is in the strong W^{1,p} norm. Theorem 2.2 and the paragraph immediately after it explain the sharp nearby context: counterexamples are known for n ≥ 4 and 1 ≤ p < ⌊n/2⌋ by using homeomorphisms whose Jacobian changes sign, while for p > ⌊n/2⌋ that sign-changing mechanism is unavailable because Jacobians of Sobolev homeomorphisms cannot change sign. That is why Open problem 3 asks whether a different counterexample may still exist for some p ≥ ⌊n/2⌋. Finally, the paper also stresses in Open problem 2 that, in dimensions n ≥ 3, approximation by diffeomorphisms and by piecewise affine homeomorphisms should not be silently treated as already equivalent.
